newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Crop prospects keep lid on Europe's feed buying.
newsitem.headline: Crop prospects keep lid on Europe's feed buying.

text.p: Feeds demand in Europe has picked up a little as prices have eased, with consumers locking in nearby cover, but the prospect of a good U.S. soybean harvest is deterring new crop purchases here, analysts said.

The firm dollar is continuing to weigh on demand and another factor near-term will be the market's hestitancy to comit itself ahead of key USDA data in two weeks' time. The USDA acreage report will be released on June 30.
"It's very quiet in the market here, everyone is waiting for the USDA report at the end of June and until then it will remain depressed," said market statistician Arie van Dijk from Stigevo.
European compound feed demand is at a very low ebb -- with cattlefeed offtake hit by the seasonal move of cows to pasture and pigfeed production by the Dutch swine fever outbreak.

The outbreak of the disease has caused the slaughter of some three million pigs in the country, around a quarter of the total pig population. The number of cases has so far climbed to around 270, a figure the Dutch Farm Minister Jozias van Aartsen has forecast as reaching 300 before peaking.
This slack demand comes at a time of increasing supply.
"There is an oversupply of products in the second half of the year led by citruspulp and cornglutenfeed and prices will be depressed as a result," Van Dijk added.
Traders said U.S. soybeans are around 90 to 95 percent planted and imports of Brazilian beans into the United States had eased somewhat the fears of tight supplies.
They also noted the USDA had raised its 1995/96 ending stocks by five million bushels to 130 million. Some reckoned this would not be last upward revision.
Van Dijk said the ending stocks could be up to 150 million bushels, bringing corresponding downward pressure on new crop prices -- as long as the weather remained favourable.
"The current price difference between new and old crop beans is just too large. These will have to converge," he said.
In addition, the good weather prospects will depress values for November beans on Chicago, currently around $6.66 a bushel.

"We could see November down at six dollars by early August," Van Dijk said, drawing a parallel with a similar market situation 20 years ago when old crop beans peaked at end-May and then new crop prices tumbled in August.

Elsewhere, traders said the lower prices for palmexpellers has sparked some consumer buying, who have been building stocks until into next year. Prices for copra products have also dropped but met little demand, they added.
